title: Alibaba to ban employees from using Anthropic's coding tool, source says

reading.body:
This is a case of a vendor instrumenting its own client software to identify how it is being used, without telling the users. The mechanism sat in the system prompt that Claude Code sends to the model, and it changed the formatting of a date string depending on the API base URL, the timezone, and the hostname. The trigger condition was a non-Anthropic endpoint, so the marker was aimed at traffic leaving Anthropic's own infrastructure rather than at ordinary users. The failure is not a model asserting something false. It is a hidden check embedded in a deployed tool, disclosed by an outside researcher rather than by the vendor.

The placement matters. The check lived in the client, on the user's machine, in code the user runs, and it activated only in the configuration used by resellers, gateways and distillation pipelines. Catching it required reading the shipped binary and noticing that a date string was being rewritten, which is the kind of detail that survives casual inspection. A published changelog, a disclosure in the tool's documentation, or a visible setting would have surfaced the same behaviour without the concealment. The obfuscation, base64 strings decoded with a fixed key, is what turned a usage check into a covert one.

Anthropic has described the tracker as an experiment and is reported to be removing it. Alibaba is reported to be banning employees from using the tool over alleged backdoor risks. Whether the code constituted a backdoor, and what Anthropic intended it to accomplish, are not established by these reports.

reports.title: Claude Code Is Steganographically Marking Requests
Anthropic is removing its covert code for catching Chinese competitors
Claude Code’s hidden tracker was an “experiment,” says Anthropic
Alibaba to ban employees from using Anthropic's coding tool, source says

summary:
A blog post reports that Claude Code version 2.1.196 contains hidden markers in the system prompt it sends to the model. A function alters the date string based on the API base URL and timezone. If the timezone is Asia/Shanghai or Asia/Urumqi, dashes in the date become slashes. If the hostname matches a decoded list of domains or AI lab keywords, the apostrophe in the date sentence changes to different Unicode characters. The domain and keyword lists are stored as base64 strings and XOR-decoded with key 91, and include Chinese tech companies, AI firms, and proxy or reseller domains.

The marker only activates when ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is set to a non-Anthropic endpoint, so most normal users are unaffected. The author suggests Anthropic likely wants to detect resellers, unauthorized gateways, and distillation pipelines, but argues the hidden approach is odd for a developer tool. The article notes the check is easy to bypass by changing the hostname, timezone, or patching the binary, and does not say what Anthropic plans to do next.
